utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We are sorry to have been late. I think it is not due to our own fault, because if the aircraft had arrived punctually, perhaps we could have kept to the time. Brother Jan was away and he was supposed to be here early this morning, but the flight from Pakistan came in late. That is why we have been delayed for so long. Mr. Niemann, we start with you, with your examination of your witness, is it not? That was where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Does your Honour wish me to announce appearances first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I expect that we will continue with Professor Economides. That is the programme we had before we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, Professor Economides -- I should say we had intended to -- we intend to call Dr. Gow; the reason for that is that Dr. Gow is restricted this week, he only has today and tomorrow to testify and that is the only time we have available to do it. We have Professor Economides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, Dr. Gow is only available today and tomorrow, and so we were anxious to start him so that we could conclude his evidence in order for the Prosecution to be able to close its case this week. The difficulty we are now confronted with is I am not sure that we will have sufficient time to conclude with Dr. Gow, unless we have some indication of how long the Defence will be in cross-examination. We will only be about two hours, I would think, in evidence-in-chief of him, but if the Defence anticipate that they will not be concluding collectively their cross-examination tomorrow afternoon, that would mean that we could not close the case, and Professor Gow would have to come back in January, because that is the only available time he has in order to conclude his evidence. So we are left with a situation whereby if he testifies and commences his evidence-in-chief now, that we all impose upon ourselves the discipline, I am talking about the Defence and ourselves, to conclude his evidence by tomorrow evening, because if he does not conclude his evidence by tomorrow evening I will not be able to close, and I do not think that it is in the interests of anybody to leave the case running now over until January. So it is unfortunate that Dr. Gow just does not have an opportunity to come back or stay longer this week. He simply cannot stay until Wednesday. I have gone over his commitments and he must go back to London tomorrow night. He is then not going to be available until very late in December, and that would conflict with times when this courtroom is going to be used in the Blaskic case. So through your Honours, may I enquire of the Defence whether they estimate that they could conclude the evidence of Dr. Gow, i.e. the cross-examination of him, tomorrow, so that I can make a decision on whether or not we should even proceed; with great reluctance, the Prosecution would not call him. We believe the evidence is of great importance and would assist the Chamber considerably on some of the matters that have arisen in the case of this Prosecution. We believe it would be most unfortunate if we had to make the decision not to call him, but unless we are prepared to impose a discipline in terms of the amount of time, then I am afraid I am left with no other option than to do that. I should say that Professor Economides is due to fly in tomorrow morning, he would not be available until lunch-time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, please? Let us have the appearances. I think you can take the Prosecutor as having announced his appearance. He has announced his appearance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are the other side of the 50 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, my partners in Houston decided I needed to come back to The Hague, which probably tells you something about my relationship with my partners in Houston.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, I am John Ackerman and I appear with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Esad Landzo. May I request your indulgence for just a moment so that Defence counsel can have a short huddle to discuss the announcement that we got from Mr. Niemann, right now, and then we will be able to respond to that announcement with some knowledge and understanding. Can we do that for just a couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (Pause). Your Honours, thank you for your indulgence. It is our very strong and considered opinion that the cross-examination of Dr. Gow would go well beyond tomorrow. Probably a good conservative estimate would be a couple of days of cross-examination. At least two Defence counsel have done significant preparation and have significant matters to cover with Dr. Gow. If I might suggest a solution, it would be that since he is here, that Mr. Niemann go ahead and do the direct examination today and that we then cross-examine him on January 12th and that should then complete the Prosecution's case and we can go from there. I do not think there is any chance in the world of completing it, unless the court is prepared to serve him with a subpoena and keep him from returning to England until he has finished his testimony. That may be a way to do it. I am certainly sympathetic to the need to get the Prosecution's case wound up. That is the only way I can think of to do it and perhaps in terms of keeping our witness reasonably happy, it may not be a good idea to put him under that kind of restraint, I do not know. We will see what the Prosecution responds to that announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution will carry on with his evidence until it is able to dispose of it. Mr. Niemann, do we have your witness, if you have anything to say about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our position, your Honour, is that we are most anxious to close the case, as we have said before. We are keen for the matter to conclude this week, which has been our position for some time. We would have hoped to have finished in early November, but we unfortunately could not get to that point, so it was really with great reluctance that the Prosecution case is extended to this point. I am loath to ask your Honours for an adjournment, and I do not believe that letting the matter go over to January is the best course. It seems that the cross-examination cannot be restricted, even if I was to endeavour to restrict my evidence-in-chief. Perhaps I could do that so that there is more time this afternoon, or if your Honours are prepared to sit for longer hours tomorrow, we may be able to conclude it; but it is with considerable reluctance that I decide not to call Professor Gow, but at the moment I am tempted to take that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I think my colleagues also agree, you can carry on with your other evidence. You need evidence as much as you can and then the Defence will also cross-examine him to the extent to which they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How long will you take with Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I had planned on taking three hours, I can reduce it to two, but I could reduce it even more than that. I would have hoped to complete it today in time for the Defence to start cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not a matter for bagging. I think they want to do their case as much as you can. You carry on with your evidence, you can certainly go ahead and do that and they would also try to do their best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. I will call Dr. Gow. (Pause). It is a considerable distance now your Honour from here to the new witness room, so it probably takes a little longer to get the witnesses down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow is an expert in military matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly swear the witness. DR JAMES GOW (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andrew James William Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you a researcher in the Department of War Studies, King's College London and a research associate at the Centre for Defence Studies, University of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hold the title of Reader in War Studies at King's College London and I am a research associate at the Centre of Defence Studies, University of London.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Formerly, were you a research officer at the Centre for Defence Studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you hold a PhD from the University of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your doctoral thesis of Yugoslavia at the School of Slavonic and East European Studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the past several years, has your work concentrated, although not exclusively, on the former Yugoslavia, particularly its military and political affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you written extensively on this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the purpose of your evidence today, have you drawn from your own writings and that of other recognised scholars in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And published reports, military and civilian writings, speeches, official documents and conversations with persons knowledgeable in this area and particularly having regard to documents made available to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you published numerous books and articles on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have published a couple of books and many articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Without naming them, have you also published monographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you participated in conferences in various locations throughout the world on a number of topics, including the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, and I have made presentations in a number of forums at the invitation of various bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you given evidence before this Tribunal on a number of occasions previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Expert Panel of the United Kingdom Security of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a member of the Expert Panel to the UK Secretary for Defence for Strategic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. Dr. Gow, what was the structure of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prior to the dissolution of Yugoslavia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslavia had a two-tier system of armed forces. One element was the regular armed force; this was designed to carry out normal armed functions, was conscript based and was intended to hold the defensive line, while the second element was mobilised. That second element was a territorial defence system organised through regional structures within the republics which constituted the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The conscript structure of the armed forces was broadly in line with the ethnic distribution of the population. The officer corps tended to be dominated around 60 per cent by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, what happened to the character of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army following the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period of dissolution, as Yugoslavia broke up and particularly as armed hostilities began, the JNA became aligned with the Serbian political leadership and alongside this, the composition of the JNA went from being something in the region of having around 40 per cent, I think it was, Serbs to being 90 per cent Serbian within a space of one to two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any relationship between the JNA and the Serbian political leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the crisis in Yugoslavia developed and as Yugoslavia broke up, the JNA leadership and the Serbian political leadership began to work together. In March 1991 there was collaboration regarding the possibility of declaring a state of emergency. As Yugoslavia came to break up, they appear to have joined forces in a project to create a new set of territories from the territory of republics other than Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the main aim of the JNA and the Serbian political leadership at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The principal aim appears to have been to create a set of territories mainly formed, but not exclusively formed, around Serbian populations in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a view to breaking the territorial integrity of those two republics and creating territories which would then be joined in a federation with Serbia. A mini Yugoslavia, but for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the attempts to achieve these aims affect all Bosnia in the same way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina was subject to this type of armed attack, it has to be said that some areas were designated to be part of this set of territories and others were not. This means in some areas there was a take-over and there were armed hostilities, in others there were not armed hostilities; but the whole of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina nonetheless was affected by this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, what military preparations were made to implement these aims prior to the commencement of the armed hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the late summer and autumn of 1991 onwards, this is with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA carried out a series of manoeuvres and exercises to mobilise Serbian reservists into units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serbian security service, the SDB, was involved in making arrangements with activists, agents in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the preparation of a political programme and also for the distribution of weapons by the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To whom were these weapons distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons were distributed to people within I think what would be regarded as loyal Serbian groups co-operating with the SDS under the influence of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was the civilian population, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be elements of the civilian population, those who had previously served perhaps in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any parallel political activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1991, a process began of marking out territory which was later to be taken to form parts of the territory of the Republika Srpska, that is the territory claimed by the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In April there was a series of declarations of associations of municipalities, given the label "Serbian". These became the basis for the declaration of Serbian autonomous regions in September 1991 in four parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A fifth area was later to be declared, I think in November. These constitute political preparations for the infrastructure for the territory which was to be carved out of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be joined with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was the objective of the JNA and the Serbian political leadership, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the objective was to establish military political control over these territories, to separate them from Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to be able to join them in a federation of a mini Yugoslavia with Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this plan confined to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not. The territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina were part of a plan to build territory around, as I said, but not exclusively, Serbian populations, and a similar pattern of events took place in Croatia prior to the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina from July 1990 onwards, with the declaration of a Serbian autonomous region of Krajina, around Knin in the Dalmatian hinterland, later followed by the declaration of a Serbian autonomous region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Srem. These two later formed the Republic of Serbia and Krajina, so the pattern was followed of declaring autonomous regions and then later declaring a republic, the intention which was to unite with this federated set of territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I just ask you to look at this document, and I have four copies for the Defence and a copy for their Honours. This document has previously been made available to the Defence, your Honour. I might indicate, your Honours, we will only be seeking to tender two documents through Dr. Gow, this one and another document. Before you comment on that, Dr. Gow, I will wait until the Defence counsel have a copy, and their Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's document 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what is the document I have just shown you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a set of instructions titled, "For the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances". It is a document prepares by the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, that is the SDS to which I made reference before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. I know Mr. Niemann indicated that this had already been provided to us. I have no memory of ever having seen this document before. It may very well have been provided long, long ago when Mr. Braskovic was still involved with the case. It certainly is not something that has been provided to us recently at all. The other thing I am concerned about with it is its authenticity. It has no signatures on it, it has no indication of its provenance other than what is stated on it. It is the kind of document that could have been prepared by anyone. I am not suggesting that it was prepared by the Prosecution by any means, I know that is not the case, but we have no idea where this came from. It could be a completely bogus document and unless the Prosecution can give us some idea of its provenance and its authenticity, then I would object to its being used by this witness in this case. It is just a typewritten document, as near as I can tell. I do not have the Serbo-Croat version, maybe it is different. I am looking at it right now and I see no signatures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have made your point. Let us hear Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document that was made available in January 16th 1997, and it is an exhibit that was tendered in the Tadic case. It was accepted in that case as a reliable document, the Tribunal accepted it there and relied upon it. I can ask Dr. Gow some questions about the document, your Honours, that he can express an opinion on, having regard to his knowledge and having regard to what he knows of this particular topic, but as I say, it is a document that was provided to the Defence a considerable time ago and as I say, it has been admitted and accepted as a document in the Tadic case. Dr. Gow, do you consider this to be a document that you would rely on for the purposes of your research and for the purposes of expressing an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why would you rely on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you mentioned, I did seek to use the document in evidence in the Tadic case and as I think I said when I was giving evidence at that time, the document -- I understand the document to have been assessed by well qualified persons from member governments of the United Nations, and on that basis, as well as appearing to me to be the way this document would be, would therefore be a reliable document to be used in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would, on the basis of that, express an opinion for it in your professional duties, you would express an opinion based on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I seek to tender it on that basis, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is admissible. I see nothing obnoxious about it being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what processes were implemented by the Serbian political leadership in order to facilitate its plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From late 1991 onwards, in addition to the steps I already mentioned, the preparations were made for the creation of what were effectively shadow governments to be prepared for the time when the plan would be put into effect. This involved the creation of crisis headquarters which made preparations for primarily the political but also some of the military aspects of the turnover, as I think can be seen from this document. This was done with two versions, one for areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which there was an absolute Serbian majority, and the other in which there was not an absolute Serbian majority. In either case, with the same view to preparing the loyal Serbs in the particular area for the turnover, and to prepare for co-ordination, for example, with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, how did the municipality of Konjic fit into this scheme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it, although Konjic was not a majority Serbian area, it was designated to become part of a Serbian territory on the basis of the number of representatives from the Serbian community in local political bodies. I am afraid I do not know what that figure is, but I also believe that the actual number does not make any difference, given that that was the basis on which they sought to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence, you spoke of the Serbian political leadership playing a role, in particular in arming the population. From your reading, did the SDS committee in Konjic play a role in arming the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the SDS in Konjic provided, distributed around 400 weapons to Serbs in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything significant happen to the JNA after the commencement of hostilities in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to the processes affecting the JNA, to which I already made reference, specifically in May 1992, the JNA formally ceased to exist. As of 19th May 1992, formally it became two armed forces, one designated the VRS, the army of the Bosnia Serbs, Vojska Republika Srpska and the other, the VJ, Vojska Yugoslavia, army of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia and Montenegro, although in fact substantially this remained the same body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what steps were taken to facilitate this end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian political leadership and the JNA command, some months prior to this action, undertook to redistribute personnel within the JNA in order that the JNA personnel serving in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be as far as possible Bosnian Serbs and that all Serbs who were not from Bosnia-Herzegovina would be transferred to units in Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who made this decision, when was it made and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision was made by Slobodan Milosevic, President of the Republic of Serbia, and Borislav Jovic, the representative of Serbia to the by then defunct or rump Federal Yugoslav State Council or Collective Presidency, and this instruction was then given to General Kidjovic, the head of the JNA, and the decision was taken by Jovic and Milosevic on 5th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was their motivation for doing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe -- judge quite clearly their motivation in doing this was to prepare for a situation in which the JNA units deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a view to carrying out the project of annexing parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina for this new state project. After, any international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independent international personality would be seen as a foreign occupying force and that therefore this decision was taken as a means of providing a way to camouflage the activity, that is to confuse the issue and to say, by formally dividing the JNA and by having primarily Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this was in fact no longer the same army, although it continued to have the same structure, and to be left with all the capabilities of the JNA as they had been in Bosnia-Herzegovina before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are there any publications or documents or other material that you have relied on in order to form this view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I relied specifically on the entry for 5th December 1991 in the selected diaries of Borislav Jovic, published as the volume, "Prozlje Medana Siflia", I think it was published in 1996, maybe 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to the expression of your professional opinion, this is something that you would regard as a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would indeed regard it as reliable. Jovic was there and knew what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to look at what I will now show you, if I may? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's document 207.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is the document you are now shown the document that you relied on in order to express your opinions you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a photocopy extract from the volume I mentioned, plus a translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, is there any particular part of the document which you say supports the opinion that you have expressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment. Your Honour, again this is a document that appears new, that we have not seen before. I have no idea where it came from, what its provenance is, whether it is really excerpts from a diary of Borislav Jovic or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Last Tuesday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do know we were served a document last week which Mr. Greaves thinks is the same language, but it appears to be a completely different document and I have no idea why it looks different today than it did last week. I am now curious about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your apprehension of its content? Is that your problem, that it might contain things which are against your interests?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course not. I have no concern whether it contains things against my interest -- I would prefer it not be used if it contains things against my interest. The issue is whether it is authentic and reliable and things of that nature. It does not look anything like what we were given last week. It may be the Prosecutor's office has retyped from what they gave us last week to make a nicer looking document, I do not know. If Mr. Niemann wants to represent that to me, that it is an accurate retyping of the document, I have no problem, other than the continuing issue of authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The understanding of authenticity is the story he tells, is it not? In what respect are you considering authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could sit at my typewriter and prepare a document that looks like this and call it the diary of Borislav Jovic; how do we know that that is what it is? That is what I am talking about as regards authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Except you have the counterpart of the diary itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not know that I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is representing to you what the diary is, that is what he is representing to you. You might follow by cross-examination later to discover whether it is a correct representation of what is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I have said, your Honour, is if Mr. Niemann says to me that what they have done is retyped the document they gave to us last week and this is the identical language then I have no problem with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Niemann is on his feet, I am sure he will be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. Perhaps I might answer the question. Firstly, in terms of whether we created, or somebody mysteriously created the document, the issue is not that, the issue is whether Dr. Gow relies on it to express an opinion. He is an expert and has testified on a number of occasions. If it is a document that he relies on to express an opinion, then in our submission that is something that is relevant. He can also express an opinion as to what he considers about its authenticity and reliability. In terms of the translated version that was given to the Defence, I am instructed that it was a -- there has been an additional typing of it. It is the same thing, but it has been retyped again, so the format may appear differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who is this Borislav Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may ask Dr. Gow to explain who he is and where he fits into the scene, he is much more expert at it than me. He is a person who, as I understand it, was there at the relevant time during the course of the conversations and after the events sat down and proceeded to write his diaries, which he published. Those diaries that he published are the material that Dr. Gow is relying on. Perhaps you might confirm for his Honour who is Borislav Jovic and how he fits into the scene, just so his Honour may know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gladly. Maybe I can clarify. I think I said already, Borislav Jovic was the Serbian representative to the State Council, also known as Collective Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and was the close political ally, collaborator, confederate of Slobodan Milosevic, President of the Republic of Serbia. I think I already said, on 5th December, as this extract indicates, 5th December 1991, Jovic and Milosevic had a discussion about the intentions regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina and took the decision that it would be advisable to transfer personnel depending on -- Serbian personnel, but depending on their origin either in Serbia and Montenegro or in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that the Serbs in the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina could then be said to be an army of Bosnia Serbs rather than the army of Belgrade, even though it was a matter of moving people around so that the same army could then carry out its operations. Maybe I could also add that although Jovic published this diary, there are relatively few copies of it available, because the Serbian political leadership, that is Milosevic, had it withdrawn from the shops at a fairly early stage, once it became clear some of the things which were in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you have read the diary as a whole. You have an excerpt of the diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have one of the few copies of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you get one of the few copies of the book, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was purchased for me by a friend in Montenegro who saved it for me until he could see me and then handed it over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I have asked the question but I will in case I have not, but this is a document that you would rely on in order to express your expert opinion on matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, you did ask me a question earlier about which part of the text I might want to draw to you. I am happy to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you go to the third paragraph of the first page of the translation, I think you will see the third sentence, and I will read just to be clear: "Practically, all those who remain in the JNA are Serbs and Montenegrins, but from all Serb lands. When Bosnia-Herzegovina is recognised internationally, the JNA will be declared a foreign" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will begin again: "Practically" -- might it be useful for the interpreters to see the original, to read with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, you are just reading short sections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Practically, all those who remain in the JNA are Serbs and Montenegrins, but from all Serb lands. When Bosnia-Herzegovina is recognised internationally, the JNA will be declared a foreign army and its withdrawal will be demanded, which is impossible to avoid." The translation is a little imprecise, it is not my own translation, it was carried out by translators in the Office of the Prosecutor, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The significance of this is the date 5th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance is that on 5th December 1991, Milosevic and Jovic foresaw what the situation would be following recognition of the independent international personality of Bosnia-Herzegovina and therefore carried out a decision to enable the overall project to be continued but in some way to attempt to be disguised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the actual decision, I think you testified earlier, took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The actual decision formally to divide the JNA into the VRS and the VJ was announced on 4th May 1992, to take effect from 19th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, how would you characterise the role of Belgrade regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The political and military leadership in Belgrade was engaged, in my judgement, in a campaign to expand the territory under Belgrade's control in the situation of the dissolution of the Yugoslav federation and the independence of some of the republics which had formed that federation; the intention was to have Serbia, Montenegro and allied federated territories from Croatia and from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the role of Belgrade one of support or was it something else, or something more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that Belgrade's role was to conceive of and to plan the execution of this project, which would see these territories carved from Bosnia-Herzegovina to be attached to Serbia or Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this include deploying military units from Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to the device I just described regarding the JNA, it also included at certain times arrangements involving paramilitary groups organised by the Serbian security service coming into Bosnia-Herzegovina and also through the period of the war, support being given by units designated VJ, that is from the elements of the old JNA in Serbia and Montenegro, going into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were affected by this war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were affected by the war, although as I think I indicated earlier, the precise way in which it was affected would depend on whether an area was easily taken over, was engaged in armed hostilities or was on the other side of the line. I think it is clear to say that as in all wars, whenever there is a major armed conflict, then the whole of the territory involved should be considered to be part of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How would you characterise the relationship between the Bosnian Serbs and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the Bosnian Serbs within the JNA and within certain political structures, and indeed associated with them, who were loyal to this project, were effectively acting in the interests of Belgrade and pursuing a course by Belgrade, although in doing that, I think they may well have been undermining what would otherwise have been a genuine political question for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they were taking the role of acting for Belgrade against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this apply to all of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not. As I think I was just trying to indicate, it was a question of those who were loyal to this project as opposed to some who perhaps took sides with the Bosnian government, others who fled Bosnia-Herzegovina and others who simply, I think, perhaps became politically disenfranchised because of this course of action. It took away what might have been a genuine political question because it was put in the framework of this armed campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How would you regard the approach taken by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina took a number of approaches, including the organisation as best they could of defence and political capabilities regarding the Bosnian Serbs in areas of conflict where there had been -- at least where there had been arming of some of the Bosnian Serbs in order to pursue this project, then I think they regarded them as potentially hostile and therefore would in some cases treat them either as prisoners of war or suspect them of being agents of Belgrade and therefore, until their status was determined, might regard them as hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did the Bosnian Serbs react politically and militarily to the international recognition of the independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs responded politically by formalising the Serbian Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was later renamed Republika Srpska in August 1992 -- sorry, in April 1992 they formally consolidated the Serbian Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which then later in August they renamed Republika Srpska, effectively declaring its association with Serbia and Montenegro through the constitution which had been enacted in January 1992, and militarily in co-operation with the JNA they began the armed campaign to secure all major communications and access points into Bosnia-Herzegovina, so as to create a frame for military and political developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the focus of the JNA operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The principal objective of the JNA and Serbian armed forces in the first weeks of the campaign appears to have been to take control of entry points or major communication points in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so in the first weeks all the major conflicts were at places such as Bijeljina or Visegrad, which, once control was taken of them, would then enable free access for Serbian movements into Bosnia-Herzegovina or, in some cases, such as Bosanski Brod, would prevent access from outside to give assistance against the Serbian campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the JNA operate in the municipality of Konjic, so far as you know from your readings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the JNA did operate in Konjic municipality. It was there for only a relatively short period of the armed conflict, perhaps until May, some time in May 1992, although once specifically JNA units had been moved out of some of the areas in Konjic, I believe bombardments using JNA artillery continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After 19th May 1992, what was the continued role, if any, of the VJ in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The VJ, that is the element of the JNA which was in Serbia and Montenegro, continued to give -- to contribute actively in terms of its personnel and in terms of supplies to the prosecution of the Serbian new state project in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It did so in a number of cases in support of the VRS, that is the JNA units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where it was necessary to provide additional support or forces of a particular kind, and it continued almost, effectively, to act as one body, albeit with a degree of operational authority given to the commander in Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Ratko Mladic. There are a number of instances over the years where VJ troops, specifically VJ troops, are identified, and a number of other cases where -- you can see even to this day a report by Ambassador Perdue; the American special representative for arms control agreements over the Dayton Peace Accords has noted one of the problems they have in the Republika Srpska that still it is effectively one army with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How would you describe then the relationship between the Bosnia Serb military command and the military political leadership in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the Bosnian Serb military command, I think I just said this, was given broad operational authority, knowing what the objectives were, to prosecute the armed campaign, and as far as possible, to do so bearing in mind not to bring Belgrade's role into question, going back to the decision by Jovic and Milosevic on 5th December 1991 to try to ensure that Belgrade would not be seen to be responsible for the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From publications and documents that you have examined and studied, did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina consider itself to be engaged in an armed conflict with a foreign army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina considered that they were engaged in armed hostilities with a foreign power. On 22nd June 1992, the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, proclaimed a state of war to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the foreign power in which it was in a state of war with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The declaration of a state of war, I believe, regarded the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so-called Serbia and Montenegro, as being the hostile power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What steps were taken by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to prepare itself for the conflict in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina began, immediately prior to the onset of major armed hostilities, began to mobilise the Territorial Defence system of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some time in early 1991 the leading party in the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDA, had also begun to prepare a shadow framework for possible developments in the future, known as the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina formally established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina appears formally to have been established on 15th April 1992, although there were also further developments taken in this regard in May 1992. These in any case were formal declarations; the reality was that the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina continued to be unformed or partially formed in this context and it was not until some time later in 1992 before a formal structure, going back to any declaration in April, began to take shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the command structure of the newly founded army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formal structure was that the presidency was supreme commander and appointed a general staff and a chief of staff. The chief of staff would then nominate commanders for regional military authorities and below that lower levels would be appointed by the chief of staff on the recommendation of reports from lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially the chief of staff was I think Hasan Efendic, but this was only for a relatively short period. On May 25th, I think it was 1992, Sefer Halilovic became chief of staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What steps were taken to achieve full mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1992, the Bosnia authorities ordered the full mobilisation of the Territorial Defence units in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this universally obeyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not, on the whole. Croats and Serbs did not respond to this call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What role, if any, did paramilitary formations play in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In ill-formed military circumstances, a number of paramilitary groups played a role on the side of the Bosnian government. Significantly the Patriotic League, which was organised by the SDA leadership, that is the Party of Democratic Action, the leading party among the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also groups such as the Green Berets -- although it is very difficult to discern exactly which units were which, because a lot of the reporting seems confused and seems generally to label all such groups as Green Berets, a lot of the time. I notice this, the UN Expert Commission report itself tends to group all the different Muslim paramilitary groups as one kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, prior to the outbreak of hostilities, was there a TO, Territorial Defence, in the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may just go back to add something to the previous answer, I got distracted in describing the problems in identifying particular paramilitary groups. The key thing was that the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, in organising the defence forces for Bosnia-Herzegovina, played a key role of being a loyalist strand, which would then create an umbrella or a framework for other elements of defence, including Territorial Defence, to be used. On this question, in Konjic, the Territorial Defence -- there was Territorial Defence in Konjic and it was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what its size was, from what you have studied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that the Territorial Defence in Konjic should have had a complement of around 2,000 personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of condition was the Territorial Defence in in the Konjic area at the outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was severely depleted. As I indicated, some, certainly Serbs and Croats, as was broadly the case, were not responding to the call, and in addition, as was also broadly the case in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA had previously moved weapons from TO facilities and concentrated them under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were the weapons of the Konjic TO stored?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that they had been concentrated in the Ljuta barracks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there weapons of other Territorial Defence units stored in these barracks, or was it just purely Konjic material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the Territorial Defence weaponry also for the neighbouring municipalities of Prozor and Jablanica had also been concentrated in the same barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, prior to the outbreak of hostilities, did the TOs have regional headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In theory, had there been an overall structure for the Territorial Defence, then there would have been regional headquarters, although the reality of the Territorial Defence system was to facilitate a large degree of autonomy at the lowest levels, because of the envisaged conflict for which the doctrine was designed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What, then, was the regional headquarters for Konjic Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The headquarters should have been Mostar, but in fact, because of the particular circumstances, was Sarajevo, was going directly -- Konjic was reporting directly to Sarajevo, as far as it was reporting at all, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What you are saying is that after the outbreak of hostilities the traditional TO headquarters, in relation to Konjic at Mostar, was not functioning, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my belief that Mostar was not being used as the appropriate point in the hierarchy regarding Konjic, but instead Sarajevo was taking that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Konjic Territorial Defence become the -- I am sorry, did the Territorial Defence become the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think as I was -- again, I tried to suggest before, there was a degree of some confusion, some transition and transformation, but the various elements, the Patriotic League, the elements of the Interior Ministry and also the Territorial Defence all went together to form the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina the only unit operational in the area, or were there other units as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the spring/summer of 1992, there were -- the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as such was not fully in existence, so the Territorial Defence units were operating, so were units of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, and, also identified, some of the kinds of paramilitary groups I made reference to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With all these groups operational, they all had their focus on the one particular enemy, I take it, at the time, or opposition in the conflict, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the spring and early summer of 1992 certainly all these units were engaged in operations against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there, from your readings, any effort made to create a joint command of these units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A joint command was formally established between the Territorial Defence, or the Bosnian army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this succeed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not appear really to have succeeded as far as it was ever functional at all, and as far as I can see there is not significant evidence to suggest that it was. After the HVO capture of west Mostar in early July 1992, relationships began to break down and certainly they did not function after that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the paramilitary units, Dr. Gow? Were they operational on the side of the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I indicated already that there were paramilitary groups operational in this area, some small particular ones, not generally well known, and also some which would broadly have been put under the umbrella of Green Berets or Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How would you characterise these paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the role of the paramilitary units was to be the guiding influence, the organisation of the most loyal strands to the SDA Muslim leadership. I say this in a context where some of the evidence is not clear, but it does appear to be that the point of organising the Patriotic League and other paramilitary groups is to provide a particular organisation of loyalists who are therefore able also to organise defence and other activities in particular areas. In a sense the framework for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina comes even not from the Territorial Defence but from the organisation of the Patriotic League, so therefore, in a way, it provides the elite or the political guidance that perhaps the JNA or the Communist Party would have been intended to provide under the old Yugoslav system, as I described the Territorial Defence system before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these similar to private armies or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in the situation it would be fair to characterise the activities of these paramilitary groups, and indeed possibly of Territorial Defence and HVO units, in some way as being private armies. It was a confused situation in which units were being formed, in which there was no overall well established hierarchy, but in which various groups were being established to co-operate to work for the same cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So having said that, how well established was the chain of command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly in the early part of the war, say May to July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I believe it was not well established and was not particularly clear in this early phase. Formal relationships did exist, but I think the degree to which all elements were integrated into one whole gives some reason to suppose that the situation was not at all clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the Konjic area in this particular period, May to July 1992, were any steps taken in relation to the military establishment, the military structure there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to the evolution and development of certain units, it was decided, or it appeared to have been decided to designate a co-ordinator to begin -- to designate a co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From the documents that you have examined, are you aware who was given that role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding from the documents that that role was given to Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps we will break for 30 minutes and continue at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (A short break) (4.35 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly invite the witness to come in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly inform the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, from your study of military matters and structures, are you able to explain how the term "co-ordinator" can be understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can attempt to offer some idea. It is not a normal term in military structures, it does not fit into a generally understood framework, although it is not a term which is without use. I think one way I would use to explain the role of co-ordinator, what a co-ordinator is, maybe would be with reference to the formation of special forces by the British during the Second World War, in which a number of small units, sometimes designated "private armies" -- indeed one of them went under the label "Potski's Private Army", began to develop for special missions. They are devised either for very special purposes or at the initiative of a particular commander, and in a situation where you have uncertain lines of command or where units do not fit into the traditional formal hierarchy of command and control, the private nature of these armies -- then I think you see the creation of the possible role for a co-ordinator there, and in the context of British special forces where these units were beginning to emerge, one man, John Hackett, was appointed with the job of co-ordinator, who incidentally went on later to be General Sir John Hackett, Commander in NATO and then after that principal of my own King's College in London. His role as co-ordinator was to know what was going on, to be able to deal with all the different units and to be sure they did not carry out private initiatives, essentially to undertake the same mission or to end up fighting each other, they call it "crossed lines", or to ensure that common resources could be created, or that logistics supplies would be made available; whatever that role particularly was. In some senses, this was carrying out some of the tasks which an officer commanding might perform, but in a situation where there was -- as not part of the formal hierarchy, there was no officer commanding at that stage, although later special forces were integrated and began to have formal officer commanding positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of authority do these co-ordinators have? You mention they must have full knowledge of what is happening, but what sort of authority did they have or exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I object to this question? I fail to see the relevancy of what the British army did in World War Two as being relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there is nothing seriously wrong with a comparative approach to any explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably there are two essential features for a co-ordinator successfully to play a role. Of course, a co-ordinator -- the term is not a usual one and therefore it is only relevant to specific circumstances, and on one level could be all or nothing, but I think it is clear if a co-ordinator's role, broadly, in any context, is to be successful, it depends on two qualities. The first would be full knowledge, that is that you would have to be able to know exactly what each of the relevant units was doing, and capable of doing, otherwise there could be serious problems in the exercise of operations; and the second is a degree of authority, perhaps personal authority, which would enable you to deal with sometimes highly charged egos of commanders of some of these particular units; that is they would have to respect you on whatever basis you had the authority, otherwise they would not give you the information, they would not trust you and you would not therefore be able to carry out your role successfully. So I think there are two elements: one is the degree of authority involved, on whatever basis the authority is founded, and the full knowledge, both of which, without being formal command roles, are consistent with some of the elements of a command position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me see. I am not too sure you have got yourself within the context of the question the Prosecutor is asking. I think if I am right the Prosecutor wants you to define a co-ordinator within the context of the Konjic municipality, or within the area in which you are here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood I was asked to give some explanation of how this term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a very broad area which you have gone into, but within the scope of your testimony, you are expected to give the military structure of the Yugoslav army, and the functions of the co-ordinator within that army and the structure he occupies. These are things which perhaps might be more helpful to us, not a general view of what a co-ordinator is, because each institution might have its own different concept of what a co-ordinator is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. If you could assist his Honour with that, particularly concentrating on the Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am happy to assist in whichever way I am able. In answering the question, I was trying to give some sense of what this term might mean and I think I stressed that it is not a usual military term, but it is one which occurs sometimes, and I was trying to give sense to definition generically, from what I know about things in the field of military matters and war, how this term might be understood. It is not a term, if you wish to ask the question regarding the Yugoslav People's Army, which was used, as far as I am aware, in the Yugoslav context normally. I am not aware of any incident where it was or that anybody understood how this role might be played in the context either of the Yugoslav People's Army or of the doctrine of general People's Defence. However, and I believe you are interested in the Konjic municipality, we did, prior to the recess, raise the question of the appointment of a co-ordinator in the Konjic municipality and I am happy to give some suggestion as to how I think that could be understood, if that is what your Honour wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was trying to express generally how this term might be understood in order then that you could look to the Konjic context in which you see a number of independently organised armed forces, i.e. the absence of a formal, organised, hierarchical command structure as you would normally expect with an armed force, and in that context, a degree of fluidity and uncertainty, and with the fluidity and uncertainty in a number of units, but the overall intention to carry out operations against the hostile Serbs, it seems to me, in designating a role of co-ordinator in the Konjic municipality, the role was based on an ability to have full knowledge and a degree of authority to be able to go to each of the various units involved and, without being able to give formal order, to be able to give guidance, to make requests, to give indications of what or what might not be appropriate and helpful in a particular situation, to see what requirements a particular unit might want and to find ways in which to satisfy those requirements. This would involve some of the capacities, some of the qualities, rather, that an officer commanding might perform in a more organised military structure, without, in fluid and changing circumstances, being a formal command position. In the Konjic municipality, and I have -- as an expert, I have only very limited knowledge of the details of the Konjic municipality itself, but I have looked at the interface between my general understanding and Konjic to address this question, it does seem to me that it is possible that the co-ordinator in question was given that role in part because of personal wealth and an ability to carry out certain tasks, including the purchase of provisions. Perhaps on the basis of personality he was able to have the trust of all sides, and I believe I saw an interview documentary in which the co-ordinator himself made this clear, that he seemed to be able to go to all sides and they seemed to trust him and be able to tell him everything accurately, again going to the importance of full knowledge for a co-ordinator; and possibly also on the basis that I understand the co-ordinator in question was also a member of the Green Berets organisation, which I think earlier, if I did not make it clear earlier, I will say, I understand to be one of the loyalist strands and therefore possibly to have a particular role in connection, vis-à-vis the central authorities or structures leading to the central authorities in Sarajevo. So it is in that context that I would explain generally the functions of a co-ordinator and in the context of Konjic how I would understand it, although I stress I do this on the basis of my general expertise and a limited degree of knowledge of looking at the situation in Konjic. I hope that has been helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At the relevant time in Konjic, there were three entities, there was the War Presidency, then there was the HVO and there was the territorial army, so the co-ordinator was appointed at that time, so maybe the co-ordinator was to co-ordinate activities of the HVO and the territorial army and also to make sure the War Presidency's orders are carried out by the other two entities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are identifying certain armed units within the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And trying to establish the relationship between the co-ordinator and the relevant units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not between the co-ordinator, between the War Presidency and the two warring factions, the HVO and the TO, so the co-ordinator was probably --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I may not be clear, but if you are suggesting that the HVO and the Territorial Defence were engaged against each other in armed hostilities at this stage, I think that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is not the case, but they were treating themselves as separate entities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly there were separate units, and also some small paramilitary groups, which were not formally designated, as I understand it, in the documentation for the co-ordinator, but I would also assume it was possible, for the co-ordinator to be able to play a role in all senses, that the role in a situation where there is no formal position of command authority, either through the structures of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in an uncertain situation and devolution of a political and military authority to the municipality in Konjic to the HVO, they were not fully participating and recognising the authority in command; therefore it does seem to me that it is relevant to look at the work of co-ordinator in the context of being able to have the trust of both sides and to deal with both sides on the basis of a degree of personal and/or other authority, to be able to say, "these are the things" -- here I am speculating, I have not looked at specific discussions, "these are the things which would be useful, or these are the things which such and such a unit might need; let us put it all together and make it more coherent".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have spoken at length about co-ordinator. Were there then subsequent steps taken later in 1992 regarding military formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are speaking with regard to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the evolution of the construction of the armed forces continued, with the designation, first of all, of seven administrative districts, which are sometimes you see referred to as corps, although I think this is not the accurate terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the corps were established, was there an intermediary period between the appointment of co-ordinator and the establishment of the corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say the seven administrative districts, I was suggesting that these were not the corps per se. Corps came to be formed at a later stage. Another development was also the creation in some areas of tactical groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is a tactical group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A tactical group, as I understand it, may as a unit -- a set of units brought together for specific tactical purposes for a temporary period. It is created in a context where the regular structures and the regular organisation of units is not judged to be appropriate to the circumstances, and it may be of what I think -- one of two types; either designed specifically for one objective in which designated units are brought together to achieve that objective, or in other circumstances to be brought together as a group in order to be able to act to some extent independently within the broad scope of objectives to be achieved, to achieve whatever is possible. I suspect that in the case of the area we are talking about, where a tactical group became relevant, Tactical Group 1, it falls somewhere between the two. The broad objective was established of actions which would facilitate lifting the siege of Sarajevo, but I have the impression that this was in an evolving context of working out what operations it would be possible to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a step in the evolution from the co-ordinator to the establishment of tactical groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand, Mr. Delalic, who had been appointed as co-ordinator, to some extent made a transition from the role of co-ordinator to being tactical group commander, after a short period in which I think it was a Colonel Polutak had been tactical group commander for a short period, but he was replaced by Mr. Delalic, who I think, as tactical group commander, again looking at the fluidity of the situation, the special circumstances, I might presume was appointed because of again the role he had already played and the authority that he seems to have had, but I say this with caution from the position of an expert, not as somebody who has looked very closely into the detail of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does the authority that a tactical group commander has, is that different from that of a co-ordinator? Can you explain the authority that a tactical group commander would have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I judge that there is a clear difference in the formal authority between co-ordinator and tactical group commander. Whereas co-ordinator, as I indicated, might carry out many of the functions of an officer commanding, a co-ordinator would not have any formal authority within the military hierarchy. A tactical group commander would have formal authority within the military hierarchy, would be able to issue orders rather than, for example, make requests or give advice, and would be backed in doing so by the regular structures of any military and the possibilities of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any further developments regarding command structures in the Konjic municipality that you looked at in the documents that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the appointment of Mr. Delalic as tactical group commander on, I believe it was, 11th July 1992, he was subsequently re-appointed on 27th July, but with a clarification or possibly an extension of the scope of his authority. A tactical group would normally be understood to have perhaps five particular units attached to it for particular operations. On 27th July, all the units in a geographical area, including Konjic, were put under the command of the Tactical Group 1 commander, so there was an evolution not only in the role played and the formal position but also in the area over which formal command authority could be said to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion as to why this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression from some of the documentation presented in evidence and that I have seen in the Office of the Prosecutor is that there may have been a degree of personal rivalry between Mr. Delalic and Captain Esad Ramic. There are a number of cases while Delalic appears to have been co-ordinator where Ramic does not respect his role fully, and there do seem to be some kinds of difference and this also seems to be the case after he has been appointed tactical group commander. I think my reading of the clarification, the superseding appointment of Delalic on 27th July, and this is only an interpretation again, a feeling from what I have seen, would be to clarify and to attempt to reinforce Delalic's formal position as officer commanding. I believe that there were some instances where Ramic disputed Delalic's authority over his particular command; "tactical group commander is not commander over me and my units because we are not assigned specifically to the tactical group". The 27th July document changes that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the next evolutionary step in the organisation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following the evolution into the creation of military districts and the establishment of some tactical groups, in November 1992, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina began finally to take shape with the creation of a corps structure, with five corps being organised through the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, answering to the general staff and command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did this affect Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Konjic municipality became -- was covered by the area of four corps in this structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Against whom was this army of Bosnia-Herzegovina engaged in armed hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage in 1992, it continued to be engaged in armed hostilities against the armed forces we were describing earlier, the divided JNA, the two elements of the JNA, and also in this period, clashes were beginning to emerge, in fact from a little earlier, between the HVO and army of Bosnia-Herzegovina units, and into the spring of 1993, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was engaged in armed hostilities with Croatian forces to the west, as well as with the forces, the Serbian forces to the north, east and south. The conflict with the Croatian forces lasted for about nine months, to the end of 1993; the armed conflict with the Serbian forces continued until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the military political relationship between the Republika Srpska and Belgrade continue after 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
