utterances.text: Yes, the military political project, to which I made allusion earlier on, to create this set of territories through the use of armed force and complementary political action continued both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, so that by May 1995 you still see some of the ways -- not only do you see ways in which Serbia and Montenegro designated forces sometimes contributing in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, but also for example in May 1995, the deputy chief of staff of the Belgrade army, that is the VJ, is appointed as commander of the Republic of Serbia and Krajina as part of the Serbs in Croatia, as a change within the one structure. In 1993 there is some speculation when the new chief of staff is being appointed in Belgrade that it will be General Mladic, commander of the element of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska. But that does not happen, I suspect partly because of the appearance it would give at that stage of the links between Belgrade and the Republika Srpska, going back to what I said earlier about the intention to disguise as far as possible Belgrade's role in all of this. You can also see the way in which, going back to the origins and the way the Serbian security service worked with the SDS and groups -- and its operatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- to prepare politically and to arm the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you see the final confirmation, in my own mind, of the way in which Belgrade could exercise control in the fact that in June 1995 the head of the Serbian security service, Jovica Stanisic is sent from Belgrade to deal with a problem which is causing a big international difficulty, the taking of UN military personnel as hostages and their being chained to ammunition dumps and other facilities, and Stanisic is the man who is able to intervene, simply to turn up with the Bosnian Serbs and everything is sorted out. Again, he plays a similar role in the later stages of the year, leading up to the process of going to Dayton for the peace talks. In all of this, I think it is clear, if I may just expand a little, I think to understand, and I believe -- my understanding is this is also something of a question of relevance, looking at the basic factual differences between this situation and another one which is of interest, I think it has to be understood that by comparison, for example, with Nicaragua, which has been raised as a case I know on a factual basis, there is a clear difference. Stanisic, the Serbian security service, the Serbian political leadership in Belgrade and the JNA leadership were exercising a role to carve territory from a neighbouring state, to change the borders through a use of force and using both their own people but particularly people in a neighbouring state, acting effectively on behalf of this project to incorporate them in a set of territories to be annexed, which it seems to me on a factual basis is wholly different from a case in which you have a group within a country seeking to change the government of the country as a whole and gaining some support from a major power, both in terms of equipment and finance and training, but in a neighbouring country, to support this overall objective of changing political power within the country as a whole -- this is in comparison with Nicaragua, where the United States, for whatever support it gave to the Contras, had no intention of either taking control of the whole of Nicaragua or indeed of annexing parts of Nicaragua, but rather for its own ideological reasons was opposed to the particular government and backed those who wanted to change the government. I think there are clear differences in the material involved in those two cases. One is the intention to annex territory and to include people as agents, if you like, in that process, and the other is the intention simply to help those who are trying change the government of a country as a whole to do so. However, whatever problems there might be with that from an ethical or other perspectives, but on a substantive basis, it seems to me there are two completely separate cases. In Nicaragua, perhaps more of a parallel would have been if the United States had been seeking to annex part of the country and had used the Anglophone, largely West African origin population on the Mosquito Coast to try to carve out a part of the country which would then be annexed as the 51st State of the Union, rather than giving support to one of the groups which is trying to change government of the country as a whole. Forgive me for adding that, it may be out of place. I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, we will proceed in this way. First counsel for Mr. Landzo. Second counsel for Mr. Mucic. Third counsel for Mr. Delic and fourth counsel for Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am hoping I am going to be able to get home, but I doubt it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have all being hoping that for months. You have only got a couple of days to worry about. My name is John Ackerman, it is obvious to you I am one of the counsel over here on this side of the room. I have quite a few things that I would like to discuss with you, and if we do not finish by tomorrow about this time then I suspect you will get to come back in January so we can finish then. We will see how we do. I will try my best to help you get out of here by 5.00 tomorrow if I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To a great extent, whether or not we will be able to do that is going to be largely dependent on you. I think you understand what I am saying to you. I am going to try the best I can, and in the context of trying to accomplish the things I need to accomplish to make my questions to you as concise as possible; perhaps many of them can be answered with a yes or no by you, but by the same token, I do not want you to think that I am trying to restrict you in some way. If you feel that an explanation is necessary with regard to a matter we are talking about, please give us that explanation, because what we are really interested in is what light you can shed on the issues we are trying to deal with here and not in trying to establish some kind of control over you that would keep you from telling us what you think is important. Do you understand what I am saying to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood perfectly. I will do whatever is relevant to assist the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, and maybe to assist me and you in getting through this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that -- I want to ask you something, just because I am fascinated by this. When I was fooling around on the Internet trying to find out things about you, one of the things I learned, and the first time we have heard it in this court that I know of, is that you are classified by King's College as a Reader and I have not seen that term before. What is that? What is a Reader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a yes or no answer, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it cannot possibly be. There will be many of them that will not be that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the British academic system, there are a number of different kinds of appointments, some which may be termed as research appointments, some which involve teaching and research, various kinds and degrees of responsibility. Leaving aside the research posts, the first level is lecturer. This is a teaching post, this is the way the majority of people enter, and they become lecturers. I was previously a lecturer in war studies, before they gave me the title of Reader. Lecturers can be promoted to senior lecturer, which usually comes as a matter of having done a number of things such as long service, having performed a number of roles in terms of college administration, teaching and research, but more or less one way. These are appointments which can be made by any of the colleges within the University of London, which is a federal body of 45 separate institutions of which King's College is one, and one of the biggest and indeed in itself it is bigger than many other universities. The position of Reader is one which denotes a degree of national recognition with the potential, possibly, for international recognition or even a degree of international recognition, particularly in the area of research and writing, and which is a title conferred not by the college but on the nomination of the college by a council of the University of London as a whole, and that council, where there is a promotion, where somebody is promoted to a senior lecturer, would nominate two referees and the process would go through and be decided. In the cases of being conferred with the title of Reader, that entails not only going through that first stage, which is the same, to get the nomination, but then further references being sought, including from people in other universities in the UK and around the world; some of which you might get a chance to nominate, some of which you just do not know, which people are then asked to confirm whether or not they think you would merit being conferred with this title. The further stage would then to be conferred with the title of Professor, that is a full Chair, which is when, as I said before, international potential or some degrees of international recognition, the sense would be overall that the work that you have carried out is of an international standing and probably you have already been a Reader or something else first. I hope that is enough of a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you have told us more about that than any of us needed to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, but you asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So one does not interpret it the way one would ordinarily interpret the term, as a description of one who sits around and reads, but it has a technical connotation that goes way beyond that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has a technical connotation which goes way beyond that and means it is difficult to find time to read, because you end up doing other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The fact people are likely to misunderstand that term would probably account for why we do not see it in your writings and your books as a description of who or what you are. We see "Lecturer", we see "Researcher", but I do not recall seeing "Reader" on any of the publications.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is because you are looking at publications for which the information was supplied before I was conferred with the title of Reader last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was only last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a course called, "the rise and fall of the Yugoslav state". Do you currently teach that course at King's College?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it a regular lecture course where students attend the course on a regular basis and you give lectures and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a course which is taught regularly, that is one of the things that I have to do on Wednesday, to be there to teach it at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of giving those students reading assignments for the kinds of things you would like them to read so that they can understand issues about the rise and fall of the Yugoslav state, I think you recommend about five works, as I can see from here. It would be a book by Ivo Banic, called, "Yugoslavia and the National Question in Yugoslavia, Origins, History, Politics"; Aleksa Djilas, "The Contested Country"; James Gow, "Legitimacy and the Military"; Susan Woodward, "The Balkan Tragedy"; and James Gow, "Triumph of the Lack of Will, International Diplomacy in the International War of Dissolution". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, is what correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That that is the essential reading that you demand of the students in that course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think it is reading that I demand of the students in the course. I am not sure what the document in front of you is. I suspect it may be a page taken either from a prospectus or from a departmental handbook. I do not recognise that, I have never seen that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Pull up your own -- not there. Some day when you get a chance, look at your college's website and you will find a description of your course and under "essential reading" it lists those five books.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was going on to say, anyway, is -- I do not know where you got it from, but I assume it is taken from a departmental handbook or prospectus, something of that kind, I guess a website, and I have to say I do not have time to visit our own college website, especially to look at my own entries on it -- that is indicative reading. I was asked, for the purpose of prospectuses and handbooks, to supply a number of books that would be relevant as introductory reading, things which people might choose to read before they came to take up the course. Probably as a normal practice, that is not the extent of the things that it is suggested people read, these are things it might be particularly useful to read before coming; it is not the only things that I recommend strongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand that where I am going with this question is just to establish that those books that you have listed as essential reading are books that you believe are useful and authoritative in terms of understanding what happened in the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that, but more precisely I would say they are useful in preparation for the course which will be taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not think you would put a book on that essential reading list that you believed was filled with inaccuracy and misjudgements and false factual matters and things of that nature. You would not want to deliberately mislead your students with bunkum, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without prejudicing one of the classes in my course, one of the things I actually do is get them to read four texts separately to form an opinion on them, at least one of which is questionable and all of which have -- because one of the important things in understanding the way I teach this course especially, but also the Yugoslav conflict as a whole, is to understand the importance of interpretations. So it is conceivable that I would put things on which I might otherwise have reservations about, precisely to bring people to points of understanding about the importance of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell me a book that you might give them that you have reservations about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The text about which I have reservations and which some poor soul who is always the fall guy has to take, is, "The Yugoslav Crisis" by John Zametica. I would stress that however authoritative and however good any text on Yugoslavia, including my own, I would never ever regard any of them as being perfect and many which have faults also have agreed strengths. For example, one of the books you mentioned there, Aleksa Djilas, "The Contested Country", is an excellent book in many respects in describing the Yugoslav Communist Party and the question of its evolution of thinking on the national question, but it is a book which in some ways I would have reservations about, particularly at the time it was appearing, the emphasis on some other questions or the way in which some questions are dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are familiar with a fellow named J.F. Brown, who wrote a book you are not particularly fond of also, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with Jim Brown and I am familiar with the book that he wrote. It is not as much that -- it is not a question of fondness, but I think you are probably going to identify that I did make a comment about his comment on my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You called him an "asinine doubting Thomas", correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did that, but that is not all that I did. I did that in the context of his having described my analysis of something -- the particular thing was that I had laid out in an article the framework for the campaign by the JNA, Serbian political military forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which I established the framework of operations and also noted the preparations which had gone before and Jim Brown, in a footnote on the book had said, if I remember correctly, and it struck a blow, I will tell you, as you understand, "but to construe planning as intention is" -- do you have the quote there? It is something like "one dimensional", I forget what, and so, piqued at this and also supplemented by the later availability of evidence from the memoirs of General Kadijevic concerning the plan I was describing, I made reference to this article and said, "this should satisfy asinine doubting Thomases like J.F. Brown", something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You and Brown basically have gone into a footnote war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think we got into anything more than a minor, and, until now, largely unnoticed, footnote skirmish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I ask you this because I am trying to evaluate the position I will be in if I tend to disagree with things you have written. I wonder if I will become an asinine doubting Thomas by disagreeing with things you have written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can we predict at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We have talked about a few books, you know that there have been a very, very large number of books written about the Yugoslav crisis and various aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look, for instance, at a list of published works about the war in Yugoslavia, the list just goes on and on, there are many, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I doubt that even you, with your focus on this, have had an opportunity to read all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It would be amazing if I had, if anybody has.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not know -- I may not be correct about this, it seems to me that if you look at those books, especially the ones that focus on the politics and the military aspects of the war and the factual matters that occurred during the war, that we might be able to divide those books into three different types. There are a group of books that were written by journalists who were active in covering various aspects of the war. I am thinking, for instance, of David Roddy's book about Srebrenica, Misha Glenny's book. There also are a group of books that were written by people who might be more appropriately classified as academics, that will include the book written by you, the new book you have just written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope it also includes the other one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is kind of old.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it is still academic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will be happy to include it. There is the book written by Susan Woodward, which tends to be written from a more academic perspective, and my understanding is that there are a whole train of academic books sitting in a line at publishers about to come out and I cannot recall as I stand here the names of those authors, but there are some people from Harvard and some other places who have some books in line. Then I think the third category would probably be people reporting their personal experiences in a role that they played in some part of it. I am thinking, for instance, of David Owen's book about his role, and I know there are several others that would fall into that category. There may be other categories, but for purposes of what I want to talk to you about, I think that is sufficient to get into what I want to talk about. There is a difference, is there not, in the discipline between, for instance, a journalist who is writing an account of incidents that occurred that they were reporting and an historian who is trying to write an academic work of history; there is a difference in the approach and a difference in -- I think difference in approach is a sufficient question. That is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There might well be a difference in approach between a journalist and an historian in the way they approached it, but I see no reason whatsoever to suppose that an historian would not be capable of writing a book as a journalist would, or a journalist an essentially historical book, or an academic book of any other description, not necessarily historical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with you that a journalist can in many ways become an historian and an historian can in many ways become a journalist, but what I am suggesting to you is the discipline is a bit different in terms of the need, if you are writing a book as an historian, from an historical perspective, to be much more certain, with regard to the facts that you report and the conclusions that you draw, that you are dealing with valid, verifiable information. A journalist might very well report, both in newspapers and in books, matters that they have heard third or fourth hand and sort of, "let the reader sort it out", sort of say, "this came from here, you decide for yourself whether this makes sense or not", whereas an historian is more likely to demand confirmations of sources and things of that nature because an historian understands they are writing not for the moment but for history.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may well be the case, it might be true of any kind of academic enterprise. I assume it is the case for history, but as I am not trained as an historian, I would be careful of expressing too firm an opinion on it. In general, an academic exercise is intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Although you are not trained as an historian, you tend to deal with history a great deal. It is a large part of what you do in terms of your writing and your lecturing and everything else. You are talking with us here today about the history of the Yugoslav crisis. You come at it from a military and political perspective, maybe like a military scientist, political scientist, but you still are coming at it from a historical perspective, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that I am. I am not sure what "coming at it from a historical perspective" means. I hate to be really difficult about this, especially seeing as I want to get away, but I really do not understand what that means. If you say that I deal with things that happened in the past as a way of understanding military and political dimensions of the present, that is the case, but dealing with things in the past is not the same thing as history.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is virtually time for us to break. Let me leave you with something that you have written. The degree of detail when you are talking about your book, "Triumph", and how it is written: "This degree of detail is necessary for an accurate interpretation rather than the more usual approach to analysis of the difficulties of the Yugoslav conflict which relies less on analysis of particulars and more on opinion, based on incomplete information and understanding." Did you get it or would you like me to read it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might as well repeat it. I think that is the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is what I will do. You are talking about the degree of detail that you go into in your book. What you have written is: "This degree of detail is necessary for an accurate interpretation rather than the more usual approach to analysis of the difficulties of the Yugoslav conflict, which relies less on analysis of particulars and more on opinion based on incomplete information and understanding." Let me ask you not to comment about that now, because I think it is time for us to break. I will give you the whole evening to figure out what you would like to say, if you have anything to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might start the comment at 10.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise. (5.30 pm)
